newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mitsubishi Motors skids to poor annual profits.
newsitem.headline: Mitsubishi Motors skids to poor annual profits.

text.p: Mitsubishi Motors Corp skidded to lower profits last business year, hit by poor sales across the globe, as major Japanese rivals raced ahead on new models and a weaker yen.
Mitsubishi, the nation's fourth biggest carmaker, announced on Thursday that its group operating profit slid 36.5 percent to 45.66 billion yen ($393 million) in the year to March 31.

Analysts said the balance sheet would have been worse without a boost in overseas markets from the weaker yen. Other top Japanese carmakers such as Toyota, Nissan and Honda chalked up strong earnings performances in 1996/97, helped by the favourable exchange rate.

"We had extremely tough domestic sales last year because of poor demand for our recreational vehicle models such as the RVR and Chariot models," Mitsubishi senior managing director Minoru Wada told a news conference.

Both the RVR and the Chariot are now four years old and sales have suffered as consumers have been attracted to newer models offered by rival makers. Mitsubishi is due to replace the models in the middle of this year.

Domestic sales of the Pajero Mini, a 660cc sport-utility vehicle launched in December 1994, fell, although demand was good for new Mitsubishi models such as Galant sedan, the Legnum station wagon and the Challenger sport-utility vehicle.
Group net profit fell 8.9 percent to 11.60 billion yen ($100 million). Net profit is equal to current profit minus taxes and extraordinary profits and losses.

Parent company operating profit also dropped 8.4 percent to 57.15 billion yen ($492 million), declining for the second year in a row and falling short of the firm's estimate of 63 billion yen ($543 million).
"The weak yen saved Mitsubishi last business year. Without profits from the weak yen, it would have been awful," said Nobuaki Yanachi, senior analyst at Kankaku Research.

Mitsubishi said it saved 59 billion yen ($508 million) as a result of the weaker yen on a parent operating profit basis in 1996/97. The average dollar/yen rate it used for settlements in 1996/97 was 111 yen against 90 in 1995/96.

Mitsubishi's parent net profit fell a steep 26.4 percent to 15.07 billion yen ($129 million) in 1996/97 due to an appraisal loss of 43.1 billion yen ($371 million) on shares owned by its U.S. sales arm, Mitsubishi Motors Sales of America Inc (MMSA).
For the current year, Mitsubishi forecast that group net profit would stay flat, but predicted parent-only net profit would bounce back by nearly 60 percent.

It forecast domestic sales of 860,000 vehicles in 1997/98, up 11.4 percent, after a 6.3 percent drop in the previous year. It estimated sales costs, which totalled 33 billion yen ($284 million) last year, would be nil this year.

Wada projected group sales of 4.1 trillion yen ($35.3 billion) for the year. Sales units in Europe and the United States were in the red in 1996/97 and would not return to the black until 1998/99, Wada said.
But analysts called the estimates too ambitious.
"They cannot achieve these projected profits and sales. They cannot reach these projected domestic sales because of stiff competition," Yanachi said.
Mitsubishi, hit by a controversy over a sexual harassment suit at its U.S. plant, said no costs had so far been incurred related to the legal action.

The case, brought by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, may be the largest sexual harassment case ever brought, with $300,000 in damages demanded for each employee. The suit alleges that the firm tolerated harassment of female employees by male workers and supervisors. ($1=116 yen)
